newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST-Femsa recovery seen firmer in Q4.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Femsa recovery seen firmer in Q4.

text.p: Fourth quarter results from Mexican food and beverage firm Fomento Economico Mexicano SA (FEMSA) will likely show the company is consolidating its recovery from Mexico's 1995 economic crisis, analysts said.

FEMSA bottles the Cuauhtemoc Moctezuma beers such as Sol, Dos Equis and Tecate, and also owns the Coca-Cola Femsa subsidiary known as KOF that bottles and distributes Coke in Mexico and Argentina. Its results are expected in late February.
Three beverage anaylsts consulted by Reuters predict a 1996 operating margin of 8.87 percent compared to 8.0 percent in 1995 and 11.1 percent in 1994.
They forecast an average 1996 earnings per share of 2.64 pesos versus 0.47 pesos in 1995. Share earnings are seen improving so much largely because of lower foreign exchange losses.
Domestic sales volumes are seen rising about seven percent and exports about five percent.

FEMSA was particularly hard hit by Mexico's 1995 economic crisis, but rising sales volumes are seen helping operating margins close in on their pre-crisis levels of around 11 percent, analysts said. Higher sales volumes in the bottling industry help margins because of high fixed costs.

"FEMSA's recovery is well under way," said Greg Rianhard, a beverage analyst with D.A. Campbell in Los Angeles. "I'm confident that FEMSA will reach my 9.1 percent margin forecast for 1996. I expect operating margins to rise near 10 percent by 1998. My estimates may be conservative."
"Investors are going to like that the operating margin is increasing," said Thomas Mobille, a Latin American beer analyst with Robert Fleming in Brazil.
Because of the fixed costs in the bottling industry, beer companies have been interested in maintaining sales volumes since the crisis, so they have not implemented real price increases.
As they did last year, FEMSA and arch rival Grupo Modelo are expected to raise prices in line with yearly inflation expectations some time late in the first quarter.
Price increases proportionally help FEMSA more than Modelo because a higher percentage of FEMSA's production is for the domestic market.

The FEMSA charge has been led by its Sol brand, which went nationwide in Mexico last year and has done well abroad, largely because of its likeness to Corona, Modelo's star export brand. Both beers, light in color and bottled in clear glass, are marketed as upscale brands.

"They're doing it mostly with Sol, which for many people is the same as Corona," Mobille said. "I was in Spain and I ordered a Corona and the guy gave me a Sol. I said, 'Hey, wait a minute, I'm a beer analyst, I know what I'm ordering.' But no one else seemed to mind."

As for KOF, analysts said they generally had less of a handle on what results to expect, in part because of signs of social discontent in Argentina, but that the operating margin should not vary greatly from the 6.5 percent of 1995.
